title: Upcasting Revisited
summary: Treating a specialized child as its broader parent type across collections and APIs.

activities.title: Everyday Analogy: The Airport Luggage Cart

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: An airport luggage cart is designed to transport any piece of 'Luggage'. Whether you place a heavy hard-shell suitcase, a nylon duffel bag, or a compact camera backpack onto the cart, the cart handles it seamlessly without requiring any modifications or special adapters. The cart only cares that the item IS luggage.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: In Java, upcasting is assigning a subclass instance to a superclass reference variable (e.g. `Luggage item = new DuffelBag();`). Because a `DuffelBag` is guaranteed to have every property and method that `Luggage` defines, Java allows this conversion implicitly (without any cast syntax) and guarantees 100% type safety at runtime.
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: Upcasting is always safe and implicit because every specialized child is guaranteed to satisfy the broader parent contract.

activities.title: Upcasting: The Engine of Polymorphic Design
activities.content:
### What is Upcasting?

**Upcasting** is casting a reference from a specialized subclass to a more general superclass or interface up the inheritance hierarchy tree:

```java
Dog myDog = new Dog();
Animal myAnimal = myDog; // Implicit upcast!
```

### Key Principles of Upcasting
1. **Implicit and Automatic**: No cast operator `(Animal)` is required. The Java compiler performs the widening reference conversion automatically.
2. **100% Type-Safe**: Upcasting can **never** fail at runtime and will **never** throw a `ClassCastException` because a subclass instance inherently possesses all state and behaviors defined by its ancestor.
3. **Interface Upcasting**: Assigning an implementing class instance to an interface reference is also upcasting:
   ```java
   List<String> items = new ArrayList<>(); // Upcasting to List
   ```
4. **Restricted View**: The only trade-off is visibility: while the object remains fully intact in heap memory, you can only access the members exposed by the superclass reference.

### Why Upcasting is Fundamental to OOP
Without upcasting, you would have to write separate methods for every subtype:
- `printDog(Dog d)`
- `printCat(Cat c)`
- `printBird(Bird b)`

With upcasting, a single method `printAnimal(Animal a)` handles all existing and future subtypes.

activities.title: Implicit Upcasting in Method Arguments and Collections
activities.explanation: Manager is upcast to Employee when passed into printPayStub(). Dynamic method dispatch ensures calculatePay() computes Alice's bonus.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: Passing `mgr` upcasts `Manager` to `Employee` without explicit syntax, triggering dynamic dispatch.

activities.title: Multi-Level Interface Upcasting
activities.explanation: An object can be upcast to any interface in its hierarchy tree. At each higher level, only that level's contract is visible to the compiler.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: Upcasting to `Printable` narrows view strictly to `print()`.

questions.question: What is upcasting in Java?
options: Converting a primitive int to double
Assigning a subclass object to a superclass or interface reference
Converting an Object to a String via (String) obj
Allocating memory on the call stack
questions.explanation: Upcasting refers to moving up the inheritance tree by treating a specialized child as a broader supertype.

questions.question: Does upcasting require an explicit cast operator like `(SuperClass) subObj`?
options: Yes, always required by Java syntax
No, upcasting is implicit and performed automatically by the compiler
Only if the superclass is abstract
Only if generics are used
questions.explanation: Upcasting is safe and widening, so the Java compiler executes it implicitly without explicit cast syntax.

questions.question: Can upcasting ever throw a `ClassCastException` at runtime?
options: Yes, if the heap is out of memory
Never, upcasting is 100% type-safe and guaranteed by the compiler
Yes, if the object is null
Yes, if the child class overrides any private methods
questions.explanation: Because a subclass is always an instance of its parent (IS-A relationship), upcasting never fails.

questions.question: Given `Animal a = new Cat();`, what happens to the Cat object on the heap?
options: It is truncated to only retain Animal fields
It remains a complete Cat object in heap memory
It is cloned into an Animal instance
It is converted into bytecode
questions.explanation: Upcasting changes only the reference type (the lens through which the object is accessed); the heap object itself is completely unchanged.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of upcasting in API design?
options: It accelerates garbage collection
It allows methods to accept and process any subtype polymorphically
It makes classes final
It eliminates virtual method tables
questions.explanation: APIs accepting supertypes (e.g. `InputStream`, `List`) can handle any existing or future subclass seamlessly.

questions.question: Which statement correctly demonstrates upcasting to an interface?
options: ArrayList<String> list = new List<String>();
List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
List list = (ArrayList) new List();
ArrayList list = (List) new Object();
questions.explanation: `List<String> list = new ArrayList<>();` upcasts the concrete ArrayList to the List interface.

questions.question: If `B extends A`, and method `void foo(A a)` exists, what happens if you call `foo(new B())`?
options: Compile error: type mismatch
Implicit upcast passes new B() as type A successfully
Runtime ClassCastException
foo is ignored
questions.explanation: Method arguments undergo automatic widening reference conversion (upcasting).

questions.question: Can you call a subclass-specific method immediately after upcasting to a superclass reference without casting back?
options: Yes, dynamic dispatch finds all methods
No, the compiler restricts method calls to those declared in the superclass reference
Only if the method is public
Only if reflection is enabled
questions.explanation: The reference type determines method accessibility at compile time.

questions.question: Given `Object o = "Hello";`, what is this operation called?
options: Downcasting
Upcasting (to java.lang.Object)
Autoboxing
Unboxing
questions.explanation: Since String inherits from Object, assigning String to Object is an upcast.

questions.question: Why does upcasting support the Open/Closed Principle?
options: It requires modifying parent classes frequently
New subclasses can be introduced and passed to existing methods without altering their signatures
It forces all methods to be static
It disables method overriding
questions.explanation: Existing modules closed for modification can accept new open extensions through upcasting.

interviewQA.question: What is upcasting, and why does Java allow it to happen implicitly?
interviewQA.answer: Upcasting is the assignment of a subclass object to a superclass reference. Java allows it implicitly because it adheres to the Liskov Substitution Principle: every subclass instance is guaranteed to support all members and contracts defined by its superclass. There is zero risk of type invalidity at runtime.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Upcasting assigns a child instance to a parent reference. It is implicit because children are guaranteed to satisfy all parent contracts.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Upcasting is safe and implicit due to the IS-A subtyping guarantee.
keyPoints: Upcasting is safe and implicit due to the IS-A subtyping guarantee.

interviewQA.question: Does upcasting modify the underlying object in heap memory?
interviewQA.answer: No. The heap object retains its full identity, all its instance fields, and its class metadata pointer. Upcasting only alters the static reference type used by the compiler to check method and field access.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: No heap changes occur. Upcasting only changes the compile-time view of the object.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Upcasting changes the reference lens, not the heap object.
keyPoints: Upcasting changes the reference lens, not the heap object.

interviewQA.question: How does upcasting enable the Strategy Pattern?
interviewQA.answer: The Strategy Pattern defines a family of algorithms behind a common strategy interface. The client holds a reference to the strategy interface. Different concrete strategies can be upcast and injected at runtime without changing the client's code or recompiling.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Upcasting allows injecting diverse algorithmic strategies into a common interface reference dynamically.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Strategy pattern relies heavily on upcasting to strategy interfaces.
keyPoints: Strategy pattern relies heavily on upcasting to strategy interfaces.

interviewQA.question: Can an array of subclasses be upcast to an array of superclasses in Java? What is this called and what danger does it present?
interviewQA.answer: Yes, Java arrays are covariant: `Integer[]` can be upcast to `Number[]` or `Object[]`. The danger is that at runtime, assigning an incompatible type into the array (e.g. `objects[0] = "text"` when the array is actually `Integer[]`) throws an `ArrayStoreException`.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Array covariance allows upcasting arrays, but can throw ArrayStoreException if an incompatible object is stored.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Java array covariance permits upcasting but risks runtime ArrayStoreException.
keyPoints: Java array covariance permits upcasting but risks runtime ArrayStoreException.

interviewQA.question: Why are Java generics invariant whereas arrays are covariant?
interviewQA.answer: Generics are invariant (`List<Integer>` is NOT a subtype of `List<Number>`) specifically to prevent the runtime errors that plague covariant arrays. Generics enforce complete compile-time type safety without relying on runtime store checks.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Generics are invariant to eliminate runtime type corruption and provide compile-time safety.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Generic invariance prevents runtime type mismatch errors.
keyPoints: Generic invariance prevents runtime type mismatch errors.

interviewQA.question: How does upcasting interact with method overloading resolution?
interviewQA.answer: Method overloading is resolved at compile time using static binding based on the compile-time types of the arguments. If you have `process(Animal a)` and `process(Dog d)`, calling `process(myAnimal)` where `myAnimal` holds an upcast `Dog` will resolve to `process(Animal)` because the compiler only sees the `Animal` reference type.
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Overloading resolution uses the reference type at compile time, not the runtime object type.
interviewQA.keyTakeaway: Method overloading is bound statically by reference type at compile time.
keyPoints: Method overloading is bound statically by reference type at compile time.

I know why upcasting is implicit and never requires explicit cast syntax.
I understand why upcasting is 100% type-safe and never throws ClassCastException.
I understand that upcasting restricts the compile-time view while leaving the heap object intact.
I know that dynamic dispatch still invokes subclass overrides after upcasting.
I understand how upcasting enables polymorphic parameters and collections.

practiceProblems.title: Warmup: Upcasting Vehicle Fleet
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Complete the fleet maintenance runner:
1. Base class `FleetVehicle` with method `public void performService()` printing `'Standard fluid inspection'`.
2. Subclass `ElectricBus` extending `FleetVehicle`: overrides `performService()` printing `'Battery pack health diagnostic'`.
3. In `main`, instantiate an `ElectricBus` and assign it implicitly to a `FleetVehicle` reference `v`. Call `v.performService()`.
Observe that upcasting happens automatically and prints the electric diagnostic.

practiceProblems.title: Polymorphic Notification Broadcaster
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a polymorphic notification broadcaster from scratch without starter code:
1. Interface `MessageSender` with method `void send(String recipient, String message)`.
2. Class `EmailSender` implementing `MessageSender`: prints `'EMAIL to ' + recipient + ': ' + message`.
3. Class `SlackSender` implementing `MessageSender`: prints `'SLACK to #' + recipient + ': ' + message`.
4. Class `AlertService` with method `public void broadcast(MessageSender sender, String target, String msg)` that calls `sender.send(target, msg)`.
5. In `Main`, create an `AlertService`, an `EmailSender`, and a `SlackSender`. Call `broadcast` once with email target `'admin@company.com'` and message `'Server high load'`, and once with slack target `'dev-ops'` and message `'Deploy complete'`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
EMAIL to admin@company.com: Server high load
SLACK to #dev-ops: Deploy complete
hints: AlertService.broadcast accepts MessageSender interface as the upcast parameter type.
Both EmailSender and SlackSender upcast to MessageSender implicitly.

practiceProblems.title: Heterogeneous Payroll Engine
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a payroll engine processing an upcast heterogeneous array of workers from scratch without starter code:
1. Base class `StaffMember` with `protected String name`. Constructor `StaffMember(String name)`. Method `public abstract double getMonthlyEarnings()` (make class abstract).
2. Subclass `SalariedStaff` extending `StaffMember`: field `monthlySalary` (double). `getMonthlyEarnings()` returns `monthlySalary`.
3. Subclass `CommissionStaff` extending `StaffMember`: fields `basePay` (double), `salesAmount` (double), and `commissionRate` (double). `getMonthlyEarnings()` returns `basePay + (salesAmount * commissionRate)`.
4. In `Main`, create an array `StaffMember[] payroll` holding:
   - `new SalariedStaff("John Doe", 6000.0)`
   - `new CommissionStaff("Jane Smith", 2500.0, 50000.0, 0.08)`
5. Loop through `payroll` and print `'Staff: ' + s.name + ' Earnings: $' + s.getMonthlyEarnings()`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Staff: John Doe Earnings: $6000.0
Staff: Jane Smith Earnings: $6500.0
hints: StaffMember[] array upcasts both subclasses cleanly.

practiceProblems.title: Bug Hunt: Array Covariance Type Leak
practiceProblems.problemStatement: The code below attempts to write an incompatible type into a covariant array, resulting in a runtime `ArrayStoreException`. Fix the code by declaring the array with the proper generic list or matching type, ensuring that all elements are valid integers and their sum is printed correctly as `'Sum: 30'`.
hints: Replace the invalid string assignment with an Integer so the underlying Integer[] is not corrupted.

practiceProblems.title: Advanced: Multi-Level Interface Pipeline
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a multi-level filter pipeline from scratch without starter code:
1. Interface `Filter` with `String apply(String input)`.
2. Interface `AuditedFilter extends Filter` with `String getFilterName()`.
3. Class `TrimFilter implements AuditedFilter`: `apply(String input)` returns `input.trim()`, `getFilterName()` returns `'TrimFilter'`.
4. Class `UpperCaseFilter implements AuditedFilter`: `apply(String input)` returns `input.toUpperCase()`, `getFilterName()` returns `'UpperCaseFilter'`.
5. Class `PipelineManager` with static method `public static String processAll(AuditedFilter[] filters, String text)`:
   - Loops through each filter: prints `'Applying ' + f.getFilterName()`
   - Applies filter to text: `text = f.apply(text)`
   - Returns final transformed text.
6. In `Main`, create an array `AuditedFilter[] filters` containing `new TrimFilter()` and `new UpperCaseFilter()`.
7. Process text `'   learn by self   '` and print `'Result: [' + result + ']'`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Applying TrimFilter
Applying UpperCaseFilter
Result: [LEARN BY SELF]
hints: Sequential transformation trims whitespace first, then converts to uppercase.
